doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Norwegian mountain ledge that inspired Trip to Pillarguri
summary: In Norway a host led him sideways along a ledge above an 1800-foot drop; Russell turned back and later wrote a tune about it.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You arrived in ’64 in Sweden. You did have one gig lined up. You met Bosse and obviously other people as well. The Concept – first of all, when George Russell goes anywhere, the Concept is right there with him.
The Concept goes with him.
You accept George, you accept the Concept.
Right.

I’m wondering, though, were there parts of the Concept – even thoughThe Concept must really be taken as a whole, were there parts of the Concept that the musicians seemed to grasp more quickly than others and that they gravitated to? That’s probably kind of a tough question, but give it some thought for a second, because I’m just curious about some of those dynamics that may have taken place at this time.

I’ll just use one. I know it was on – there was a festival in Norway. I don’t know whether they still have it, Norwegian jazz festival. It comes out of Oslo, but the festival site is up into a more mountainous and very dramatic side of Norway, very beautiful, just clear water and . . .
It sounds like an inspiring venue.
Mountains that went up to the sky.
That sounds lovely.

It was funny, but when you get to Norway, one of the very first things they do is, they say, oh, we want you to see something. You go with them. They take you up to a mountain that’s like maybe two miles high. Then they take you out to a rock that juts out of the mountain, all to test your manhood.
Your sense of adventure and fearlessness, huh? That’s interesting.

I remember one day going to this – the woman I was going with at the time. Her sister had married, and this fellow took me up to one of those mountains. Everything was fine. We drove up. Then we walked out on this ledge. Then he decided to walk down, instead of we’d drive back. Let me – I kept noticing that he wasn’t walking straight. He was walking with his hands on – his hands were touching the mountainside.
Oh, okay. So he was using his hands to steady himself.
Touching the mountainside. The reason he had to walk down that way, sideways, with his hands touching, was because there was an 1800 foot drop.
Was he on a ledge?
An 1800 foot drop going down. He grew up in that country, and they’re used to that. But I kept looking, and the space between the mountain and you was narrowing.
So it was a ledge kind of situation.
So it’s not only . . .
He was going sideways, you say.
You had to go sideways to get down the mountain that way. That meant that you were looking down 1800 feet.
Did he go all the way down like this?
No. The reason he didn’t is because it didn’t take me long to say, hey, you got it, uh-uh, no.
Because you started out with him when he decided to go. Okay. I didn’t get that at first.
I had to say an end – I wrote a song about it, a tune called Pillarguri.
That’s what that’s about. I knew that was a name of something, but – what does that mean, or what is it the name of?
Pillarguri was – when Swedes invaded Norway, the Norwegian army had posted this woman to be a lookout. This is where she stood, on top of this . . .
At Pillarguri?

. . . at Pillarguri. She stood on top of the mountain, so that when – was it the Swedes? It may have not been the Swedes. Maybe it was – no, I don’t think it was the Germans that they were warring with. But it seems to me more likely that they would have been Swedes.
The area has a history of a lot of internecine . . .
She was to give a warning when these people came in that district. She did, and the Norwegians captured the Swedes and made slaves of them.
So this is a place of history.
Trip to Pillarguri. That’s – I had to call it, because . . .
Trip to Pillarguri.
. . . I got cold feet. You don’t know what it’s like to be up there . . .
1800 feet.

. . . and this guy’s a mountaineer. He’s a doctor too. Would have needed a doctor. He had the guts – to him – he must have done this a lot of times, because he was very careful. You had to be very careful with your steps. See a space about – this is the mountain, and you’ve got a space.
Not very wide.
Not very wide. It’s about two feet, and then nothing.
Drop, sheer drop.
Sheer drop. So it wasn’t exactly my cup of tea.
